catalog_quote: 4.2 Phonological word. The phonological word in Chong may also be called the stress-groups. [...] There are three types of phonetic stress in Chong language : strong, weak and unstress. The strongly stressed syllable is defined as a syllable which is loudest and longest in duration. It always occurs on the major syllable. [...] The weakly stressed syllable [...] always occurs on the presyllable which has a final consonant. [...] The unstressed syllable [...] occurs in an open presyllable with a neutral vowel. [...] Since stresses are predictable in word, they are not phonemic and they are not marked in the phonemic transcription. [...] 4.2.1 Word structure. The word in Chong is described in terms of syllable which are marked by stress occurring on the syllable. The last syllable is always the nucleus which has strong stress. The peripheral syllables are weak stress or unstress. [...] 2)…

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened the copy we hold (260-pp image-only scan from sealang.net Mahidol archive; scanned pages in the page image) and rendered PDF pp. 49-50 and 127 to images to check against the page itself, not just the scanned. Thesis p. 34 (PDF 49), sec. 4.2 'Phonological word', reads exactly as quoted: 'The strongly stressed syllable is defined as a syllable which is loudest and longest in duration. It always occurs on the major syllable. It is marked by [ ' ] in phonetic transcription. The weakly stressed syllable.. It always occurs on the presyllable which has a final consonant.. The unstressed syllable.. It occurs in an open presyllable with a neutral vowel.. Since stresses are predictable in word…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is predictable and non-contrastive: primary ('strong') stress always falls on the final syllable of the phonological word, which is the major (full) syllable; preceding presyllables are weakly stressed if closed (CVC) and unstressed if open with a neutral vowel. Words are monosyllabic ('s), sesqui/disyllabic (u's, w's) or rarely trisyllabic (w u's / u,w's). Register (4-way phonation contrast) is the lexical suprasegmental; stress is not.
new_statements.secondary_stress: A 'weak stress' [,] is assigned to closed presyllables (e.g. [,team 'khin] 'woman', [,luk ka'mo:j] 'salt'); open presyllables with schwa are unstressed. In the single u,w's example /praja:'ma:n/ 'enemy' the weak stress is on the second (open, long-vowel) presyllable.
new_statements.exceptions: None to final stress; trisyllables are rare and partly Thai loans; 4.2.2 notes variation (presyllable reduction/dropping) in disyllabic words. Same final-stress rule stated for the Wang Kraphrae (Pong Nam Ron) dialect, ch. V pp. 111-113.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the 'phonological word' (= stress group) in a tagmemic hierarchy below the intonation group; statements are based on citation-form wordlist elicitation with phonetic transcriptions of isolated words and short sentences.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement (ch. IV) describes Khlong Phlu Chong (Khlong Phlu village, Khao Khitchakut district, Chanthaburi) -- the central/northern Chong dialect area, squarely within chon1284 (same dialect zone as Edmondson 1996 and near DiCanio's Takhian Thong and Huffman's Thung Saphan, Makham). Ch. V of the same thesis gives the identical rule for Wang Kraphrae Chong (Pong Nam Ron district), the divergent southern dialect, also under ISO cog / chon1284. The held Noppawan 2003 thesis is on Kasong (Trat), a distinct Pearic variety that Glottolog files under chon1284's bibliography; it was not read.

new_statements.quote: The majority of the words in Kasong are either monosyllabic or disyllabic. The trisyllabic words are rare. The syllable structure in the word can be summarized as: C(C) V (C). 'C(C) V (C) There is only one main stress which occurs on the major syllable at the end of word. The presyllable is always unstressed and the pitch level is neutral. (p. 11) [...] The suprasegmental features in Kasong are complex since this language is in a transitional stage of becoming a tone language. From my data, the pitch contrasts (low, mid and high) are found as well as the voice quality contrasts (clear and breathy). [...] In this study I decided that Kasong is a language with three tones as follows. (p. 12)

Adds that the variety described has a three-tone system co-existing with final stress. Identity caveat: the work describes Kasong = 'Chong of Trat' (Borai district, Trat province), which the author, following Suwilai Premsrirat (2000, 2001), treats as a language distinct from Chong of Chanthaburi (different vocabulary, final /-l/ and cluster /sr-/, preverbal negation, weak breathy voice); Glottolog nevertheless files it under chon1284 (the saved chon1284 page links 'Kasong at WALS', and the PuRe record tags the thesis ISO 639-3 c…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are mono- or disyllabic (sesquisyllabic: presyllable + major syllable); the single main stress falls on the major syllable, i.e. the last syllable of the word, and the presyllable is always unstressed with neutral pitch. Independently of stress the author analyses Kasong as having three tones (clear mid, clear high, breathy low) on the major syllable, calling the language transitional toward a tone language.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None: the author states there is 'only one main stress'; presyllables are always unstressed. No secondary stress mentioned.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Trisyllabic words are said to be rare and are not discussed; the presyllable shows consonant fluctuation (/s/~/th/, /k/~/m/) but this does not affect stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Kamnuansin 2002 describes Kasong, the 'Chong of Trat' spoken in Ban Khlong Saeng, Ban Padaw and Ban Dan Chumphon, Danchumphon subdistrict, Borai district, Trat province (data 2000-2001, mostly speakers over 55). The author argues (pp. 4-6) that Kasong is a different language from Chong of Chanthaburi (lexical differences, final /-l/ and /sr-/ cluster, negation before the verb, no double negation), citing Suwilai 2000/2001; Glottolog 5.3 still lodges Kasong under chon1284 (Chong of Chanthaburi) via its WALS 'Kasong' link, and the PuRe record tags the thesis ISO 639-3 cog. The catalog's existing statement (Siripen 2001) is about Khlong Phlu / Wang Kraphrae Chong in Chanthaburi. Any site entry should label this quote as Kasong (Chong of Trat).

sources.note: Sec. 4.2 'Phonological word' (pp. 34-40): three phonetic degrees (strong, weak, unstress); strong stress always on the major syllable = last syllable of the word; weak stress on closed presyllables, open presyllables with neutral vowel unstressed; stress predictable, not phonemic. Word types 's, u's, w's, w u's, u,w's. Same rule restated for Wang Kraphrae Chong, sec. 5.2-5.3.1 pp. 111-113 ('The nuclear syllable.. takes a strong stress. It always occurs in the final syllable of the phonological word').
